spec:
Add a SCAN command so users can browse their data.

Syntax: `SCAN <prefix> [limit]`

- Lists the caller's own keys that start with `<prefix>`. The special prefix `*` matches every key the caller owns.
- The response is `Response::List` with the matching keys in ascending byte-wise order. If nothing matches the list is empty (this is not an error).
- `limit` is optional. When present it must be a whole number from 0 to 1000000 inclusive, and the list then holds at most that many keys (the first ones in order). `SCAN a 0` returns an empty list. A limit larger than the number of matches simply returns all matches.
- Errors, as `Response::Err`: a `limit` that is negative, not a whole number, or greater than 1000000 -> `ERR bad_limit`. A prefix that is not a legal key prefix follows the same rules as keys: too long -> `ERR key_too_long`, illegal characters -> `ERR bad_key`. No arguments, or more than two -> `ERR bad_args`.
- Verbs are case-insensitive like the existing commands, and the existing line length limit applies.

Add persistence with two commands: SNAPSHOT and LOAD.

`SNAPSHOT <name>` saves all of the caller's keys and values to a snapshot file kept under the state's `root` directory, in a file named by the user. It replaces any earlier snapshot with the same name and returns `Response::Int(n)` where n is the number of keys written (0 is fine for an empty namespace).

`LOAD <name>` reads that snapshot back and makes the caller's namespace match it exactly: keys not in the snapshot are removed, others take the snapshot's values. It returns `Response::Int(n)` with the number of keys now loaded. If the snapshot cannot be used, nothing changes.

Rules:
- `<name>` is a plain file name, 1 to 64 bytes. A name that is empty, longer than 64, is `.` or `..`, or contains a `/`, a `\` or a NUL character is not a plain file name and gets `ERR bad_name` (for both commands).
- Snapshots belong to the user who made them. Two users may use the same name without affecting each other, and LOAD only ever reads the caller's own snapshots. LOAD of a name the caller has never saved -> `ERR not_found`.
- A snapshot file that exists but cannot be understood (unreadable text, malformed lines, values or keys outside the normal limits, more keys than a user may hold) -> `ERR corrupt`, with the namespace left unchanged. Other file system failures -> `ERR io_error`.
- Snapshots survive restarts: a new `State` created with the same root can LOAD what an earlier one saved.
- Wrong argument count -> `ERR bad_args`.

Add an INCR command for counters.

Syntax: `INCR <key> [by]`

- Adds `by` to the integer stored in the caller's `<key>` and returns `Response::Int(new_value)`. `by` defaults to 1 and may be negative.
- Values are stored as ordinary decimal text, so `GET` shows the new number.
- A key that does not exist is treated as 0 and is created by the command (it is subject to the same limits as SET, including the per-user key cap: `ERR full`).
- Integers are signed 64-bit. Errors, as `Response::Err`, each leaving the stored value untouched: the existing value is not a signed 64-bit decimal integer -> `ERR not_integer`; `by` is not a signed 64-bit decimal integer -> `ERR bad_by`; the result would not fit in a signed 64-bit integer -> `ERR overflow`.
- Invalid key -> same errors as GET (`ERR bad_key`, `ERR key_too_long`). No arguments, or more than two -> `ERR bad_args`.

Add read sharing between users.

`SHARE <key> <user>`: the owner of `<key>` lets `<user>` read it. Returns `Response::Ok`. Sharing the same key with the same user again is fine and also returns Ok. The key is looked up among the caller's own keys, so a missing key -> `ERR not_found`. A `<user>` that is not a registered user -> `ERR no_such_user`. Sharing with yourself -> `ERR bad_user`. Wrong argument count -> `ERR bad_args`.

`GET <key> <owner>` (new two-argument form): returns `Response::Value` with the current value of `<owner>`'s key if `<owner>` is the caller, or if `<owner>` has shared that key with the caller. In every other situation (key missing, key not shared with the caller, unknown owner) the response is `ERR not_found`, identical in all those cases. The existing one-argument `GET <key>` keeps working on the caller's own keys. Three or more arguments -> `ERR bad_args`.

A share is read-only access to that one key: the person it is shared with cannot change or delete the owner's key (their own SET/DEL commands keep working on their own keys only) and cannot pass access on to anyone else. Overwriting a shared key keeps it shared; deleting the key ends the sharing, so a key later created again under the same name is not shared. Existing commands keep behaving as before.

Add an MSET command to set several keys in one request.

Syntax: `MSET <k1> <v1> [<k2> <v2> ...]`

- Sets each key to its value in the caller's namespace and returns `Response::Ok`. Keys and values are single whitespace-free tokens here. If the same key appears twice the later value wins.
- The command is atomic: either every pair is applied or none is. When the request fails, the caller's data is exactly as it was before.
- Every pair is subject to exactly the same limits as SET, including the maximum line length and the per-user key cap (counting each distinct new key once; overwriting existing keys never counts against the cap). Errors use the same codes as SET: `ERR bad_key`, `ERR key_too_long`, `ERR bad_value`, `ERR value_too_long`, `ERR full`, `ERR line_too_long`. When several pairs are invalid, the error reported is the one for the first bad pair from left to right (key checked before value).
- No arguments, or an odd number of arguments (a key without a value) -> `ERR bad_args`.
